6.122.m:
Kārttikeya said:
O lord, tell specifically now the fruit of the row of lamps (Dīpāvalī).
For what purpose is it performed, and who is its deity?

And what should be given there, and what should not be given, tell [me], O lord.
What delight is prescribed here, and what sport is proclaimed here?

Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Skanda, the blessed one who dried up Kama,
praising Kārttika, O brahmins, said this, laughing:

The holy Śiva said:
In the dark fortnight of Kārttika, on the thirteenth day, O fire-born,
one should offer a lamp to Yama outside; [thereby] premature death is destroyed,

[saying]: 'May the son of the Sun along with Mṛtyu, holding a noose in his hand,
and together with Kāla and his wife, be pleased by the gift of a lamp on the thirteenth.'

And in the dark fortnight of Kārttika, on the fourteenth day at moonrise,
a bath must certainly be taken by those who fear sin.

On the fourteenth day overlapping the previous tithi in the other-than-bright fortnight
of Kārttika, at the time of dawn, one should take a bath unslothfully.

Lakṣmī resides in oil, and the Gaṅgā in water, on the fourteenth of Dīpāvalī.
Whoever takes a bath when it has arrived does not see the world of Yama.

Apāmārga, and likewise tuṃbī, prapunnāṭa, and āhvāla,
one should circle around during the bath for the destruction of hell,

[reciting]: 'Joined with a clod from a furrow, endowed with thorny leaves,
remove sin, O apāmārga, being swung repeatedly!'

One should circle apāmārga and prapunnāṭa over one's head.
And then water-libation should be performed with the names of the king Yama:

'To Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, and to the Ender,
to the son of Vivasvat, to Kāla, and to the Destroyer of all beings,

to Audumbara, to Dadhna, to Nīla, to Parameṣṭhin,
to Vṛkodara, to Citra, and to Citragupta, salutation!'

Having worshipped the deities, a lamp should be offered for [averting] hell.
Then, at the time of twilight, one should offer charming lamps,

especially in the abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others,
in storehouses, sacred trees, assemblies, and at rivers,

on ramparts, in gardens, reservoirs, main streets, and inner gardens,
in quiet stables and also in elephant stalls.

Thus, at the time of dawn on the new-moon day, O fire-born one,
having bathed, and having worshipped and bowed to the gods and ancestors with devotion,

and having performed the pārvaṇa-śrāddha with curds, milk, ghee, and so on,
and having fed the brahmins with various kinds of foods, one should ask their pardon.

Then, at the time of afternoon, one should nourish the citizens, O dear one;
a king, having held an assembly with them, and having paid respect and conversed,

inspires their affection for up to a year, O Guha.
Before Hari awakens, women should first awaken Lakṣmī.

When a man awakens Lakṣmī with a virtuous woman at the time of awakening,
Lakṣmī does not abandon him for an entire year.

Having obtained fearlessness from the brahmins, the enemies of the gods who feared Viṣṇu,
knowing him asleep in the Ocean of Milk, and likewise Lakṣmī resting on a lotus,

[recited]: 'You are light, fortune, sun, moon, lightning, gold, and star.
That light which is situated as the light of the lamp, the light of all lights,'

'the Lakṣmī who is on earth on the auspicious day of Dīpāvalī,
and in the cowshed at the Kārttika full-moon, may that Lakṣmī be the granter of boons to me.'

Śaṅkara and Bhavānī sat down to gambling in sport;
Lakṣmī, who was situated in the form of a cow, was worshipped by Bhavānī.

Long ago, having been defeated in gambling by Gaurī, Śambhu was stripped naked and dismissed;
hence this Śaṅkara became miserable, while Gaurī always remained in happiness.

He whose victory comes first has happiness for a year.
When midnight has arrived thus, and the eyes of people are half-shut in sleep,

then Alakṣmī is driven out from the courtyard of the house
by the women of the city, delighted, with the playing of wind-instruments and drums.

In case of defeat, the opposite would occur. On the first lunar day when the sun has risen,
in the morning, Govardhana should be worshipped; one should practice gambling at night.

Likewise, cows should be adorned, and spared from carrying and milking,
[praying]: 'O bearer of Govardhana, support of the earth, savior of the cowherd station!'

O you who were raised up by Viṣṇu's arm, become the granter of ten million cows!
Whatever fortune belongs to the world-guardians, standing in the form of a cow,

and bearing clarified butter for sacrifices—may she take away my sin!
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me; / may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows."
Thus the worship of Govardhana: / Satisfying the gods, virtuous men, and mortals with sincere disposition, / others with food and drink, and the learned with gifts of speech,
the residents of the inner apartments with garments, betel, lamps, / flowers, camphor, saffron, and various edible delicacies and dishes;
the village bull with gifts, the vassals with wealth, the king [should gratify], / and the hosts of foot-soldiers with beautiful necklaces and bracelets;
the king should separately delight his ministers and his kin. / Having duly gratified them, then [he should watch] wrestlers, actors,
bulls and great oxen fighting with rivals, / and other kings, warriors, and foot-soldiers fully adorned.
Mounting a platform himself, he should watch actors, dancers, and bards; / he should cause fights, and lodge cattle, buffaloes, and the like;
he should attract calves with cows through shouting and roaring exchanges. / Then, in the afternoon, in the eastern direction, [or] toward the south-east,
he should fasten a road-barrier to a fortress post or to a tree— / a divine [rope] made of kuśa and kāśa grass with many pendants, O Guha.
Having shown them, he should lead elephants and horses beneath the road-barrier, / along with cows, bulls, buffaloes, and female buffaloes noisy with bells.
He should have the road-barrier fastened by eminent twice-born who have performed the fire offering. / Then the observant vow-keeper should make obeisance with this mantra:
"Obeisance to you, O guardian of the path, granter of happiness to all worlds! / Underneath the road-barrier, O Skanda, go cows and great bulls,
kings, royal princes, and especially brāhmaṇas. / Stepping across the road-barrier, may they be free from sickness and happy!"
Having done all this, at night he should perform worship of Bali, lord of the Daityas, / in bodily form on a maṇḍala drawn on the ground.
Painting Bali, king of the Daityas, with five colored pigments, / complete with all ornaments, accompanied by Vindhyāvalī,
surrounded by Kūṣmāṇḍa, Maya, Jambha, and the Dānava Madhu, / complete, with a cheerful face, a crown, and large earrings,
having the two-armed king of Daityas depicted, inside his own / house, in a spacious hall, he should then worship him,
delighted, along with mother, brothers, and kinsmen, / with lotuses, white water-lilies, kalhāra flowers, and red lotuses;
with perfumes, flowers, cooked rice offerings, along with milk-and-jaggery puddings, / with liquor, meat, spirituous drinks, licked foods, sucked foods, edible dishes, and offerings.
Accompanied by his minister and royal priest, with this mantra the king / who performs the worship will indeed have happiness for a year:
"Obeisance to you, King Bali, O lord, son of Virocana! / Future Indra, enemy of the gods, please accept this worship!"
Having thus performed the ritual of worship, he should keep a vigil at night; / he should arrange festive shows at night with actors, dancers, and singers.
Common people too, at the entrance of the house, with an offering of white rice, / having set up King Bali, should worship him with fruits and flowers.
Dedicated to Bali, all [acts] should be performed there in the sacred fire. / Whatever [gifts] the seers who see truth declare imperishable—
whatever gift is given here, whether small or great, / all of that becomes imperishable, auspicious, and pleasing to Viṣṇu.
"Men who will perform your worship, O Bali, at night— / may all unvedic piety belong to you!"
And pleased, Viṣṇu himself, my child, granted again to Bali / a great festival beneficial to the asuras.
From that time forth, O general, the Kaumudī festival has always been observed, / driving away all afflictions, destroying all obstacles,
dispelling the sorrow of the world, desirable, bringing wealth, prosperity, and happiness. / By the word 'ku', the earth is understood; 'muda' means joy; thus both [are present],
and by verbal derivation in sacred texts as well; therefore it is called Kaumudī. / Because on the earth people rejoice mutually with diverse emotions,
glad, content, and attaining happiness—therefore it is called Kaumudī. / Because white water-lilies are offered to Bali upon it, O Six-faced One,
by kings for the removal of sins, my son, therefore it is called Kaumudī. / For just one single day and night, every year in Kārttika,
the surface of the earth was given to the king of Dānavas like a mirror. / For a king who performs it in his realm, whence can fear of disease come?
Abundant food, well-being, health, and supreme prosperity are his; / and all the people are free from disease, devoid of all afflictions.
Therefore Kaumudī is celebrated to produce good disposition on earth. / In whatever state of mind one remains on this day, O Six-faced One,
be it joy, sorrow, or any other, his year passes in that way indeed: / if weeping, the year weeps; if rejoicing, the year is joyful;
if well fed, he will be an enjoyer for a year; if healthy, he will remain healthy. / Therefore Kaumudī should be celebrated by auspicious men with joy.
And this lunar day in Kārttika is declared both Vaiṣṇava and Dānava.

Those who observe the Festival of Lamps, bringing delight to all people, and worship King Bali with auspiciousness— / for families possessing gifts, enjoyment, happiness, and intelligence, the entire year passes into joy and great prosperity.
O Skanda, these lunar days, beginning with the second and so forth, are renowned; / and after four months during the rainy season, they bring auspiciousness:
the first in the month of Śrāvaṇa, the next in Bhādrapada, / the third in the month of Āśvayuja, and the fourth in Kārttika.

The one in the month of Śrāvaṇa is 'Kaluṣā' (defiled), that in Bhādrapada is 'Malā' (impure), / in Āśvina it is 'Pretasaṃcārā' (roaming of spirits), and in Kārttika it is 'Yāmyakāmatā' (granting desires of Yama).
Guha said: / Why is that one called 'Kaluṣā'? Why is it considered 'Nirmalā'? / Why is that one 'Pretasaṃcārā'? Why is it renowned as 'Yāmyā'?
Sūta said: / Having heard these words of Skanda, the Blessed Lord, author of creation, / smiling, spoke gentle words, the bull-bannered god.
Maheśa said: / Formerly, when the slaying of Vṛtra occurred and Purandara attained the kingdom, / a horse sacrifice was undertaken to remove the guilt of killing a brāhmaṇa.
The sin of killing a brāhmaṇa was shattered by Indra in anger with his thunderbolt; / divided into six parts, it was cast down upon the earth—into trees, water, and the ground,
into women, into the killer of an embryo, and into fire, distributed in due order. / Prior to hearing that sin, on the day of the second lunar day,
women, trees, rivers, the earth, fire, and the slayer of an embryo / became defiled; for that reason it is known as Kaluṣā.
The earth formerly sank into the blood of Madhu and Kaiṭabha; / it is pure [below] eight inches, but for women the menstrual flow is impurity;
all rivers are soiled during the rains; the soot above the fire is impurity; / trees are soiled with sap; those who slay an embryo are impure by association.
Defilements wander on it; therefore it is considered Kaluṣā. / Blasphemers, atheists, and rogues who disparage gods, seers, ancestors, and dharma—
it was purified from the pollution of their speech, and therefore the second is Nirmalā. / Those who teach and study the scriptures on forbidden days of study,

Followers of Sāṃkhya, logicians, and followers of the Veda—from the blemish born of their spoken words and ungrammatical words,
she was purified on the second lunar day, and therefore she is 'nirmalā' (spotless).

Through Kṛṣṇa's birth, O child, the three worlds are purified.
In the month of Nabhasya, that lunar day was designated as 'nirmalā' by the wise.

The Agniṣvāttas, the Barhiṣads, the Ājyapas, and also the Somapās,
[move] among the fathers and grandfathers; because of the movement of the spirits of the dead (pretas), she is 'pretasaṃcarā'.

The fathers are indeed called pretas; and on that [lunar day] occurs their movement.
Worshiped by sons, grandsons, and daughter's sons with svadhā mantras,

satisfied with offerings at funeral rites and sacrifices, they depart; hence [she is] 'pretasaṃcarā'.
During Mahālaya, the movement of the pretas is seen upon the earth.

Therefore is she called 'pretasaṃcārā', O peacock-mounted one [Kārttikeya]!
Because worship of Yama is performed on this [day] by men, O fire-born one,

therefore she is called 'yāmyakā'; truly, truly it has been spoken by me.
Those best of men who hear this Kārttika-glorification,
the merit born of bathing in Kārttika is assuredly theirs.

On the second lunar day in Kārttika, one should worship Yama in the forenoon.
A man who bathes in the daughter of the Sun [the Yamunā] does not see the world of Yama.

On the second lunar day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika, O Śaunaka,
Yama was formerly fed in her own home and honored by Yamunā.

On that second lunar day, there was a great release and the denizens of hell were gratified;
freed from sins, they were released from every bond.

Comforted and contented, they all remained at their own pleasure.
A great festival occurred for them, bringing happiness to the realm of Yama.

Hence this Yama-dvitīyā is renowned across the three worlds.
Therefore, O brāhmaṇa, the wise should not eat in their own home on that day.

One should eat with affection from the hand of a sister, which increases nourishment,
and gifts should be bestowed upon sisters in accordance with the rule,

together with gold, ornaments, garments, worship, and hospitality.
One should eat above all from the hand of a sister born of the same mother.

Eating from the hand of any sister increases strength.
On the bright second lunar day in the month of Ūrja [Kārttika], Yama was worshiped and propitiated.

Mounted upon the buffalo-seat, the lord who wields a staff and club,
surrounded by joyous servants—obeisance to that one whose self is Yāma!

Those by whom sisters and married women living in the family home are pleased through gifts of garments and the like,
for a full year have no quarrel, nor any fear from an enemy.

Auspicious, renowned, granting long life, the means to achieve dharma, desire, and wealth—
all this, together with its secret, has been explained by me, O sinless son.

On the lunar day on which the god Yamarāja was fed by Yamunā out of sisterly affection,
whoever eats from his sister's palm on that lunar day in this world obtains wealth, good fortune, and the highest prosperity.

6.123.m: how the practice of the vow should be performed by men according to rule, / how it is begun originally, and how it is properly concluded;

how many in number it should be performed, speak of that to me, O Maheśvara!
Tell me this vow in detail, O best of the gods, O sinless one.

The glorious Rudra said:
Well said, O Pāvaki! I shall tell you all that you have asked, O sinless one.
Listen with devotion as I speak, O best among the intelligent!
Just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, the sun among luminous bodies, / Meru among mountain peaks, and the son of Vinatā among birds;
just as the Gaṅgā is among holy places, and the merchant among subjects; / even so is the month-long fast the best of all vows.
Whatever merit is found in all vows, in all holy places, / and whatever arises from all gifts, the observer of the month-long fast obtains.
Through various sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant priestly gifts, / one does not attain that merit which comes from fasting for a month.

He has chanted, offered oblations, given gifts, practiced austerities, and made ancestral offerings—
that man who performs fasting for a month in accordance with the rule.

Having intended a sacrifice to Viṣṇu and thoroughly worshiped Janārdana,
and having received the guru's permission, one should then observe fasting for a month.
Having performed all the meritorious Vaiṣṇava vows as prescribed, / such as the twelfth-day observances, one should then fast for a month.

Having performed the Atikṛcchra, the Pārāka, and then the Cāndrāyaṇa penances,
one should observe the month-long fast after ascertaining the strength and weakness of one's body.

A forest hermit, or an ascetic, or a woman, or a widow, O sage,
should then perform the month-long fast with the permission of a guru or a brāhmaṇa.

Having fasted on the eleventh lunar day in the bright fortnight of Āśvina,
one should undertake this vow for thirty days.
A man who, having worshipped Vāsudeva, fasts for the entire / month of Kārttika shall partake of the fruit of liberation.

In Acyuta's abode, with devotion, at the three junctions of the day, with auspicious white water-lilies,
with fragrant mālatī blossoms, blue lotuses, padma lotuses, and kamala lotuses,

anointing [him] with saffron, vetiver, camphor, and excellent sandal pastes,
he should worship Janārdana with food offerings, incense, lamps, and the like.

With mind, action, and speech, one should worship the one whose banner bears Garuḍa.
A man, a woman, or a widow undertaking it, endowed with great devotion, with senses subdued,

should indeed converse day and night about Viṣṇu's names alone;
with devotion, praise of Viṣṇu should be uttered, free from false conversation.
Endowed with compassion for all beings, of peaceful conduct, non-injurious, / whether sleeping or seated outdoors, he should glorify Vāsudeva.

Keeping in mind that perfumes and the like in the world are tasted and celebrated,
one should avoid mouthfuls of food and the consumption of morsels.
Anointing the body, anointing the head, betel, and cosmetics— / one observing the vow should abandon all these and whatever else is forbidden.

One observing the vow should touch nothing, nor disturb anyone engaged in improper action;
remaining in a temple of the deity, even a householder should practice the vow.
Having performed the month-long fast according to the prescribed rule, / a man, a woman, a widow, or a virtuous wife should worship Vāsudeva.

Thus the vow lasts for thirty days, neither less nor more.
Having observed the month-long fast with mind restrained and senses conquered,
he should then worship the holy Garuda-bannered deity on the twelfth lunar day; / he should worship him with flower garlands, perfumes, incense, and ointments.
With garments, ornaments, and musical instruments a man should please Acyuta; / he should bathe Hari with devotion using water from sacred tirthas and sandalwood.
His limbs anointed with sandalwood, adorned with incense and flowers; / and having fed the best of brāhmaṇas with gifts of garments and the like,

he should give them a priestly gift and, bowing down, ask for their forgiveness.
Having asked the brāhmaṇas for forgiveness, having bidden farewell, and having revered and honored them,

thus according to one's wealth, endowed with devotion, and according to one's ability,
having indeed performed the month-long fasts and worshiped Janārdana,

and having fed the brāhmaṇas, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus at the end of the month-long fast, having chosen thirteen brāhmaṇas,
he should then dismiss them; hear by what rule: / Having fasted on the eleventh lunar day, he should cause a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice to be performed.
Having worshipped the Lord of gods, Hari, with the permission of the preceptor, / and having honoured Him according to one's ability, and likewise having saluted the guru,
one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas preceded by obeisance— / those of pure family and conduct, intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped all thirteen and having fed them, / [giving] betel, pairs of garments, food, and clothing,
and indeed having given meditation-cloths, cords, and sacred threads / to the best of Brāhmaṇas, having honoured them and bowed down,
one should then worship with devotion a bed prepared with coverings, / provided with a sheet, auspicious, excellent, with pillows, and adorned.
Having fashioned an image of oneself out of gold according to one's means, / one should place it upon that bed after worshipping it with garlands and the like.
A seat, sandals, an umbrella, a pair of garments, two shoes, / and sacred flowers—these one should place upon the bed.
Having thus dedicated the bed and prostrated before those Brāhmaṇas, / one should pray for assent: 'May I go to the world of Viṣṇu.'
Then the person goes to the beloved, sorrowless realm of Viṣṇu. / To those Brāhmaṇas seated in the pavilion this must be spoken repeatedly:

'O best among the twice-born, whatever is lacking in mantra, lacking in devotion, or lacking in ritual action— / may all that attain completeness by the grace of your word.' / Thus the rite of the month-long fast has been duly proclaimed.

6.124.m: Īśvara said: / Hear the glorification of Prabodhinī, which destroys sins and increases merit, / granting liberation to those whose intellects know reality, O best of the gods!
The Bhagīrathī Gaṅgā roars on earth only as long / as the sin-destroying Haribodhinī in the month of Kārttika does not arrive.
Sacred bathing places and lakes as far as the ocean remain effective only as long / as Viṣṇu's lunar day, Prabodhinī, in the month of Kārttika does not arrive.
[The fruit of] thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices / is obtained by a single fast on Prabodhinī.
Whatever is difficult to obtain and hard to reach in the three worlds, movable and immovable— / even that, when prayed for, Pratibodhinī grants, O Brāhmaṇa.
Sovereignty, worldly life, knowledge, kingship, and the wealth of happiness— / Haribodhinī, when fasted upon, grants these with ease, O Brāhmaṇa.
Sins equal to Mount Meru and Mandara that have been accumulated— / Haribodhinī burns them away by a single fast.
Whoever naturally performs a fast on Prabodhinī / according to the injunction, O tiger among men, obtains the stated fruit.
Whatever sin has been accumulated across thousands of previous births / is burned away by keeping vigil on Prabodhinī, like a heap of cotton.
Hear, O six-faced one, I will declare the characteristic marks of the vigil, / by merely knowing which Janārdana is no longer hard to attain:
singing, instrumental music, dance, and reading the Purāṇa; / incense, a lamp, food offering, flowers, fragrant ointments;
fruits, guest-water, faith, charity, restraint of the senses, / accompanied by truth, free of sleep, endowed with joy, accompanied by rites,
with wonder, with enthusiasm, free from sloth and the like, / accompanied by circumambulation and the like, preceded by obeisances,
accompanied by waving of lamps with an unwearied mind— / performing the waving of lamps to Hari watch after watch, O fortunate one.
Endowed with these qualities, one should keep vigil for the all-pervading Lord; / he who does so with a single-pointed mind is not born again on earth.
Whoever thus keeps vigil on Viṣṇu's day with devotion / and without fraudulent withholding of wealth, is led to the supreme state.
Whoever constantly worships Hari in Kārttika with the Puruṣasūkta— / Keśava has been worshipped by him for thousands of crores of years.
Worshipping daily in Kārttika according to the rule / declared in the Pañcarātra, a person becomes a sharer in liberation.
Whoever worships Hari in Kārttika saying, 'Salutation to Nārāyaṇa,' / is released from the torments of hell and goes to the sorrowless abode.
Whoever reads the thousand names of Hari and the Liberation of the Elephant King / in the month of Kārttika does not experience rebirth.
For thousands of crores of yugas and hundreds of manvantaras, / one who keeps vigil on the twelfth day in the month of Kārttika dwells in heaven.
Those born in his family by the hundreds and thousands / attain the abode of Viṣṇu; therefore one should keep vigil.
Whoever sings a hymn in the final watch of the night in Kārttika / dwells in Śvetadvīpa together with his ancestors, O noble lady.
Offering food to Hari at the end of the day in Kārttika, / one dwells in heaven for as many yugas, O best of sages.
Endless is worship with mālatī flowers and lotuses, O tiger among sages; / he who worships the Lord of the lords of gods goes to the supreme abode.
Having observed the eleventh day in the bright fortnight of Kārttika, / and having given auspicious water-pots in the morning, a person goes to my abode.
Kārttikeya said: / O Lord, let the holy, supreme vow among vows be declared, / which is to be performed by you in the month of Kārttika, namely Bhīṣmapañcaka.
Its procedure and its fruit as well, O best among the gods— / declare them to me by your grace, O grandfather of the sages.
Īśvara said: / I shall declare that most holy vow, O best of the wise; / since this five-day vow was obtained by Bhīṣma
from the presence of Vāsudeva, it is called Bhīṣmapañcaka. / Who, except Keśava, is capable of stating the virtues of this vow?
Hear the ancient dharma in the bright fortnight of Kārttika, / practised by Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Garga, and others in the Kṛta age and subsequent ages,
and by Ambarīṣa, Bhoga, and others in the Tretā age and subsequent ages; / by Brāhmaṇas with celibacy, through recitation, fire offerings, rituals, and the like;
and by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas devoted to truth and purity. / It is difficult to perform for those lacking truth, impossible for the simple-minded.
They declare it difficult, fearful; it cannot be done by ordinary men. / The one who performs it, O lord of Brāhmaṇas, by him everything is accomplished.
And this vow is greatly meritorious, destroying major sins; / therefore the Bhīṣmapañcaka should be performed with effort by human beings.
Having bathed properly according to the rules in the bright fortnight of Kārttika, / one should undertake the five-day vow on the eleventh day.
Having bathed particularly in the morning and likewise at midday, the practitioner of the vow, / at a river or a mountain stream's pool, having applied cow dung,
should properly satiate the ancestors in order with barley, rice, and sesame seeds. / Having bathed, observed silence, wearing washed clothes and firm in vows,
giving water to Bhīṣma and offering guest-water with effort, / worship of Bhīṣma must be performed, and gifts should be given diligently.
Having carefully given five jewels especially to a Brāhmaṇa, / the Lord Vāsudeva united with Lakṣmī is also always to be worshipped.
Having worshipped during the five-day period, one is satisfied for crores of kalpas; / whatever is done should all be arranged fivefold.
One obtains the entire fruit of the vows of a whole year / by giving water and also offering guest-water.
The person who does so with this mantra becomes a sharer in liberation.
"To him of the Vaiyāghrapāda lineage, with the Sāṅkṛtya ancestry, / to Bhīṣmavarman, who has no son, I offer this water."
"To the incarnation of the Vasus, the son of Śaṃtanu, / to Bhīṣma, a lifelong celibate, I offer this arghya."
Thus the mantra for the arghya offering: / He who completes the five-day observance according to this rule / obtains merit equal to a horse sacrifice; there is no doubt about this.
The observance must be kept with effort, even for the five days; / without an observance, O son, no result comes from the ritual of a vow.
Hari gave [this] to Bhīṣma when the northern course of the sun was lacking; / even without the northern course of the sun, auspicious purifications and ascendant signs [are obtained].
Then one should worship the god Hari, the remover of all sins; / immediately after, one must carefully perform the Bhīṣmapañcaka.
With devotion one should bathe him with waters, with honey, milk, and clarified butter, / and likewise with the five products of the cow, and with fragrant sandalwood water.
Then one should smear Keśava, who has the banner of Garuḍa, / with fragrant sandalwood, with saffron, and with camphor mixed with uśīra grass.
One should worship him with lovely flowers accompanied by incense and fragrances; / the devotee should burn bdellium resin mixed with clarified butter for Kṛṣṇa.
One should offer a lamp day and night during the five days and the like; / one should present excellent food as an oblation to the god of gods.
Thus having worshipped the god, having remembered and bowed down to him, / one should chant "Obeisance to Vāsudeva" one hundred and eight times.
And one should sacrifice with sesame, rice, barley, and the like smeared with clarified butter, / reciting the six-syllable mantra accompanied by "svāhā."
Having observed the evening twilight rites and bowed down to him whose banner is Garuḍa, / having chanted the mantra as before, the practitioner of the vow should sleep on the bare ground.
All this procedure is to be performed for five days; / but listen to the specific rule in this vow that makes it complete:
On the first day, the practitioner of the vow should worship the feet of Hari with lotuses; / on the second day, he should worship the region of the knees with bilva leaves.
Next, he should worship the head of the discus-bearer with jasmine; / on the full moon of Kārttika, with devotion, fixing his mind on the god of gods,
having briefly worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa on the eleventh day, / having consumed cow dung properly, he should fast on the eleventh day.
The practitioner of the vow should consume cow urine on the twelfth day, with mantras, seated on the ground, / and indeed milk on the thirteenth, and curd on the fourteenth.
Having consumed [these] for the purification of the body, fasting during the four days, / having bathed on the fifth day and worshipped Keśava according to the rule,
the wise man, casting aside sinful intentions and keeping celibacy, / should feed brāhmaṇas with devotion and give them a priestly gift.
Renouncing liquor, meat, and sin-producing sexual intercourse, / feeding on vegetables or hermits' wild grains, a man devoted to worshipping Kṛṣṇa,
should then eat at night preceded by [consuming] the five products of the cow; / when it has been properly completed in this way, he obtains the stated fruit.
Even a drunkard who drinks wine from birth until the end of his life / reaches the supreme abode by performing this vow of Bhīṣma.
Women should perform it on the word of a brāhmaṇa to increase their merit; / and widows should perform it to enhance the happiness of liberation.
For the fulfillment of all desires and for merit, O Fire, / those who observe Kārttika with daily bathing and giving gifts,
and devoted to meditating on Viṣṇu, should perform the vaiśvadeva sacrifice; / it bestows health and sons, and destroys great sins, O child.
One should observe Kārttika at sacred places with all effort, O six-faced one; / the completion of the vows of the year is recognized to be in Kārttika.
An image of sin should be made, very terrifying, in fierce garments, / holding a sword in hand, stepping forward, with iron fangs, frightening,
placed upon a measure of sesame seeds, wrapped in black cloth, / with a garland made of red flowers, and wearing shining golden earrings.
Having worshipped it with supreme devotion using the names of Dharmarāja, / taking a handful of flowers, one should pronounce this mantra:
"Whatever sin was committed in another birth, or again in this birth, / may it be completely pacified through the grace of your feet."
Having thus worshipped that golden image according to rule, / having worshipped to the best of one's ability the brāhmaṇas who recite the Veda,
for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa, the god of gods, whose deeds are unwearied, / it should be given to a brāhmaṇa, saying, "May Dharma be pleased with me."
A priestly gift should be given to the reciter according to one's capacity; / one should give gold and cows, saying, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me."
Having accomplished his purpose, remaining detached and self-restrained, / he should also give excellent gifts to others according to his ability.
With a peaceful mind and free from fault, he attains the supreme abode. / Dark as a blue lotus petal, four-fanged and four-armed,
eight-legged, single-eyed, with spike-like ears and a braying voice, / sluggish, double-tongued, copper-eyed, covered in a lion's hide,
Mahādeva, who has no [ordinary] form, is thus to be meditated upon. / This was told to me by Bhīṣma while he lay on the bed of arrows.

This difficult Bhīṣmapañcaka has been recounted to you by me, / blessed, meritorious, sin-removing, the great vow, O Yudhiṣṭhira, / by performing which the killer of a brāhmaṇa and the killer of a cow are freed from all sins.
The vow known on earth as the Bhīṣmapañcaka, spanning from the eleventh to the fifteenth, / is declared for one who does not eat; Viṣṇu bestows an auspicious reward on that vow of abstinence.
Sūta said: / This has been performed in the world as the greatest merit, difficult to obtain; / this secret, a compilation of the essence of the scriptures, has been told by me.
It was kept secret from all the gods, very hidden, and bestowing liberation; / and hearing it, at once, O goddess, even those devoted to having sex with forbidden women,
a seller of a daughter, or a seller of a sister—it liberates both. / This scripture bestows liberation; it should not be revealed to other people.
Hearing it, a person goes to liberation in an instant; / it should be carefully concealed, and as for those men who have renounced,
the merit is not spoken to them; it is true, true, O six-faced one. / Thus all this has been declared: the fruit of Kārttika.
Glorious Viṣṇu said: / Thus it was spoken by the god of gods to his son for his welfare; / hearing that statement of his father, the six-faced one was filled with joy.
With joined palms, they all said to that god who is the life of the universe: / "We have achieved our purpose upon hearing the fruit born of Kārttika;
there is nothing else to be heard; the fruit of my birth has been attained." / Having heard this glorification, whoever worships the reciter,
with cows, land, gold, and clothes, is indeed equal to Viṣṇu; / for when the reciter is worshipped, Viṣṇu is worshipped.
Therefore one should always worship him if one desires auspicious success. / The dharma treatise, the Purāṇa, and whatever is Vedic knowledge,
the book should be given only to the reciter by one desiring merit; / givers of Purāṇic knowledge indeed enjoy endless fruit.
He who recites this with devotion, or having heard it retains it, / is freed from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Wealth, grain, fame, sons, longevity, and health / are obtained merely from hearing this glorification; there is no doubt.

Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the glorification of Kārttika, / in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā, ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter.

6.125.m: The sages said: / Sūta, O Sūta of great fortune, wishing for the welfare of the world, / you have recounted the narrative of Kārtika, which grants worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now tell us the glorification of Māgha, O Lomaharṣaṇa, / by hearing which the great doubt of people is destroyed.
By whom was it revealed in this world in ancient times, O fortunate one? / Declare that glorification of bathing in Māgha together with its legendary history.
Sūta said: / Excellent, excellent, O best of sages! You are devoted to Kṛṣṇa, / since, filled with joy, you repeatedly ask with devotion about the stories of Kṛṣṇa.
I shall narrate the glorification of Māgha, which enhances merit / and destroys sins for people who hear it and for those who have bathed at dawn.
Once, O brāhmaṇas, Pārvatī, endowed with modesty, / having touched his lotus feet, questioned Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
Pārvatī said: / O God of gods, O Mahādeva, granter of fearlessness to devotees, / be pleased, O Lord, ruler of the universe! Speak now what I ask.
Diverse duties have been heard from you previously by me, O omnipresent Lord; / now I wish to hear the glorification arising from Māgha. Speak of it!
Indeed, by whom was it performed in ancient times? What is the rule? Who is the deity? / Tell all of that in detail, since you are affectionate to devotees.
Maheśa said: / Having bathed at the concluding ablution of a sacrifice, with auspicious rites performed by sages, / honored by all the citizens, there went out from his own city
Dilīpa, best of kings, a ruler fond of hunting, / filled with eagerness and surrounded by an array of hunters.
With shoes on his feet, wearing a blue turban and armor, / with an arm-guard of iguana skin bound on, bow in hand, creeping stealthily,
with archers bound with small swords and foot-soldiers equipped likewise, / in the very lovely and extensive forests of the Gāndhāras,
having crossed great streams, that young man with the prowess of a lion / sporting joyfully with them in the thickets, hunted wild beasts.
"Let this deer be struck! Let it be struck! Indeed, this one is fleeing!" / shouting thus to his servants, he himself bounded up and struck.
He went here and there, looking around at the forest tract: / crowded with flocks of peacocks frightened and flying up onto branches or hiding,
terrified by herds of does, with young running in all directions, / in places terrifying with the loud howling and shrieking of jackals,
in places bearing, as it were, the splendor of elephants through herds of rhinoceroses, / in places resonant with the screeching of owls nestled in hollows,
stamped here and there with the paw-prints of lions, / and in places reddened with the blood of blue bulls torn by tigers' claws,
and in places suggesting, as it were, the grounds of a palace courtyard / with sleek female buffaloes afflicted by the weight of their plump udders,
in places thickly covered with trees and fragrant with wild flowers, / in places having entrances like bower cottages, lovely with the humming of bees,
dreadful with large caverns of serpents whose sloughed skins were half cast off, / and dreadful with boas lying concealed in holes, sloughing their skins,
in places glowing with the flames of forest fires, bright with the luster of rocks, / filled with hissing sounds, teeming with deer and tigers.
Releasing his pack of hounds here and there after hares / and resting near pools of water, he went further into the depths of the forest.
As the king was thus advancing and the group of hunters bounded along, / making a great noise, an antelope emerged from the forest.
It covered the ground on a difficult path with the speed of its leaps; / sometimes it seemed to have mounted the sky, and sometimes it was on the ground.
Following its tracks, the king entered a rugged forest / with twisting, very deep streams, crowded with thorny trees.
Having gone further and further into a desolate region from country to country, / his throat and neck dried up from the exertion of chasing the unseen deer.

His mouth and palate were copper-red, he was bathed in sweat, his foot-soldiers were exhausted, his voice faltered; / having traversed long roads, afflicted with thirst when the sun was at the zenith,
he saw before him a lake rivaling the ocean, / situated by shores of dense trees, an excellent, pure, and auspicious holy bathing place,
spacious, with full-blown lotuses, intoxicated with honey and bees, / covered with the green leaves of lotuses as if with emeralds,
with fish leaping freely, pure as the mind of a virtuous man, / mingled with moving aquatic creatures, adorned with rows of ripples,
cruel inside with throngs of crocodiles, like the mind of wicked men; / impassable in places with moss, like the house of a miser; / assuaging the distress of diverse birds day and night,
like a generous giver who destroys the misery of the afflicted with all his possessions; / satisfying wild beasts with its waters as if they were its own ancestors.
removing all distress, as the cool-rayed moon removes the heat of the day. / Seeing him, he became free from weariness, like a cātaka bird seeing a rain-cloud.
There the king drank water, performed his midday rites, / and having eaten the game meat along with his companions, the ruler
dwelt on the shore of the lake, narrating pleasant tales. / Then, having fitted an arrow to his bow, he stayed in a tree at night.
The hunters, taking up their positions, blocked the paths in all directions. / While the warriors stood thus, having spread their nets in the forest,
at midnight a herd of wild boars came out along the shores, / and having grazed on the roots by the lake, fell into the midst of the hunters.
Those boars were struck by the king, and many were killed by the hunters; / in an instant those boars fell pierced upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing them, the hunters, exceedingly proud, made a tumultuous roar; / running and filled with joy, they assembled where the king was.
Taking them along with his soldiers, he once more departed from the bank of the lake; / wishing to go to his own city, he saw an ascetic on the path:
a brāhmaṇa, an elderly descendant of Harīta, adorned with the conch and discus, / his body emaciated by difficult and severe observances,
reduced to bones, highly restrained, with glowing and coarse skin, / wearing a deer skin and clad in soft bark garments,
chanting Vedic prayers, bearing nails, bodily hair, and matted locks. / Seeing that forest hermit, the king respectfully gave way,
and bowing with his head, stood with folded hands held like a lotus. / Then the twice-born sage, recognizing him as a king by his ornaments,
spoke for the sake of his welfare, out of a desire to help others: / "For what purpose, O king, at this most auspicious and holy time,
in the month of Māgha, are you going away, completely forsaking the morning bath in the lake?" / The king then replied: "I do not know, O best of the twice-born,
what the fruit of the Māgha bath is. Relate that to me in detail!" / Hearing these words of the king, the Vaikhānasa sage said:
"The venerable sun, dispeller of darkness, is quickly rising. / This is our time for bathing, O king, not an occasion for conversation.
Having bathed, go and ask that Vasiṣṭha, the lord of your family." / Having said this, the silent ascetic went forth for the morning bath.
Having turned back, Dilīpa too bathed there according to the injunctions; / then that heroic king, filled with joy, returned to his own city.
Then, having reported to his inner apartments the account of the forest ascetic, / he mounted a chariot with white horses, attended by a bright white umbrella and chowries.
Adorned with ornaments, finely clad, and surrounded by his ministers, / he heard repeatedly the shouts of victory and was praised by Māgadhas and bards.
He went to Vasiṣṭha's hermitage, remembering the sage's words, / and bowed there to the brahmin sage with humble and courteous conduct.
Offered a seat, having received the guest offering, and adorned with blessings, / when the king was joyfully asked about his welfare by the sage,
then the king, delighting the sage's heart, spoke a word; / handsome in form, he asked what had been spoken by the forest hermit.
Dilīpa said: / 'O lord, by your grace I have heard in detail / conduct, political ethics, and whatever other royal duties [there are],
and the rites of the four castes and stages of life, / gifts and their rules, sacrifices and rites,
the vows enjoined for them, and likewise the worship of Viṣṇu. / Now I wish to hear what fruit there is in the bath of Māgha; / tell me, O brahmin sage, what is to be performed according to rule.'
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'Rightly has the supreme good, which brings welfare to the three worlds, / been spoken of by that sage who dwells in the forest as a means of purification.
Even those drawn close and whole by the glances of charming women / desire to bathe in a stream when the sun is in Capricorn.
Without fire, without sacrifice, without sacrificial rites and pious deeds, O dear one, / they desire a good state by bathing at dawn in outdoor water during Māgha.
Those who, without giving cattle, land, gold, rubies, golden cows, and the like, / desire [the same fruit] by bathing in Māgha in a single body of water, O king—
those who desire heaven without emaciating their bodies / through three-week observances, kṛcchras, and parāka penances, always bathe in Tapas.
Worship of Hari in Vaiśākha, and austerity and worship in Kārtika [are praised]; / but in Māgha, the triad of austerity, burnt offering, and gift is distinguished.
An earthly ruler would surely undergo a great revolution, accompanied by its consequences, / by which intellect productive of absolute liberation might not arise again.
That service to the lotus-like feet [of Hari] has been enjoined by those with divine sight; / inexhaustible is that austerity and gift in the month of Māgha, O best of kings.
Whether with desire or for the sake of offspring, or dedicated to Hari, or even without that, / one who observes the vow of bodily purity obtains the fourfold fruit of bathing.
Fasting from food, Aditi bathed in Māgha for twelve years / and obtained twelve sons, the Ādityas, who illuminate the three worlds.
Rohiṇī became fortunate, Arundhatī became habituated to giving, / and Śacī, endowed with beauty, [obtained residence] in a seven-storied mansion from Māgha.
In a courtyard made pure and splendid, delightful with female dancers, / secluded from the varieties of the continents, filled with beautiful women,
resounding with singing and musical instruments, adorned with auspicious customs, / purified by the sound of the Vedas, and adorned by learned brahmins,
devoted to the worship of the gods, charming, and ever serving guests, / they dwell rejoiced here, by whom a bath is taken when the sun is in Capricorn,
by whom much was given in Māgha, and Murāri was worshipped and praised / through renunciation of desired things and through the keeping of an observance.
Māgha, the constant source of dharma, cuts off the root of sin; / grounded in desire through its fruit, when desireless it always bestows knowledge.

Whatever worlds belong to those of wise conduct, whatever worlds belong to forest-dwellers,
whatever worlds belong to devotees of Viṣṇu—those always belong to those who bathe in Māgha.

Men return from the world of the gods by other merits, O scorcher of foes;
those devoted to the Māgha bath never return.

A mortal who, having bathed in Māgha, gives a milch cow,
for as many hairs as she has on her entire body, O best of kings,

for that many thousands of years he is glorified in the heavenly world.
He who, performing the Māgha bath, gives sesame seeds with jaggery,

having washed away his sin, that man shines stainless.
Of all heaps of grain, sesame seeds destroy sins.

Therefore, in Māgha sesame seeds should be given with effort, O best of kings.
Performing the Māgha bath, one should give a meal to a brāhmaṇa.

Having gratified the ancestors, pure in soul, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, with every effort, Māgha is spent in giving.

One should never pass Māgha without giving gifts, O best of kings;
knowing one's wealth, one should always give gifts in Māgha according to one's means.

He who performs the Māgha bath and gives sandals and water pots
to brāhmaṇas remains firmly in heaven.

Performing this supreme austerity consisting of the Māgha bath, O king,
one should never pass it without giving; heaven is obtained through giving.

Heaven is attained through giving; happiness is attained through giving;
sin born of great crimes is destroyed through giving, O king.

Austerity without giving does not shine, just as the sky without the sun,
or a lineage without offspring, or a house without proper conduct.

There is nothing more purifying or sin-destroying than this,
which was sung to a Vidyādhara by Bhṛgu on the Jewel Mountain.

The king said:
O brāhmaṇa, when did the brāhmaṇa Bhṛgu speak on the mountain
and give this instruction on dharma to him? Please tell me out of curiosity.

When the region between the Himālaya and the Vindhya had then become desolate, O king,
deprived of svāhā, svadhā, vaṣaṭkāra, and the recitation of the Vedas,

when that world was afflicted, devoid of dharma, and lustreless,
and the circle of the earth was void of fruits, roots, food, and water,

having departed together with his disciples from his delightful hermitage on the bank of the Revā, shaded by trees at the foot of the Vindhya,
Bhṛgu went to the Himālaya.

There stands a mountain to the west of Mount Kailāsa,
known as Maṇikūṭa, a mass of gold, gems, and rock.

Down below it was white with crystal, in the middle the mountain was of blue stone;
white on all sides with ashes, it shone like Nīlakaṇṭha.

Everywhere composed of blue stone, with streaks of gold interspersed,
it shone like a dark cloud flashing with streaks of lightning.

The mountain had blue stone at its summit and a golden girdle below;
it appeared like Nārāyaṇa robed in yellow garments.

Having a dark-blue luster up to the slopes, with white stones here and there in the middle,
that mountain shone like the sky filled with stars.

Having obtained its bright form, bearing blazing divine herbs
and producing much radiance, it shone like a second moon.

On its plateaus, with the singing of Kinnarīs accompanied by whistling reeds,
and with the banner-like leaves of plantains, that mountain always looks splendid.

With emeralds, lapis lazuli, rubies, and crystal stones,
with their halos of radiant rays, that mountain seemed surrounded by rainbows.

Adorned with gold made of all minerals and with various gems,
with its very lofty peaks it seemed encircled on all sides as if by flames of fire.

Coming upon its ridges and grassy rocks,
Vidyādharīs, distraught with passion, lament their husbands.

Having blocked the inner passages of the breath, having conquered distress, dispassionate ones
meditate day and night on Brahman upon its delightful ridges and in caves.

Siddhas, rosaries in hand, their eyes half-opened,
worship the Lord of beings in the beautiful caves.

The quarters of space are perfumed with the fragrance of mandāra flowers,
and it is always resonant with the murmuring sound of the waters of torrents.

With young and wild elephants playing in the valleys,
and with herds of musk deer, and beautiful dappled deer,

with playful herds of yaks, and various beasts of prey,
and with calling pigeons, cakoras, and cuckoos,

and with royal swans and peacocks, that mountain is always delightful,
constantly served by gods, Guhyakas, and troops of Apsarases.

The king said:
Full of many wonders is this mountain, the refuge of all perfections.
O venerable one, how great is its height, how great its length and breadth?

The Ṛṣi said:
It is thirty-six yojanas in height, ten yojanas at its summit
in length and breadth, and sixteen yojanas at the base.

Adorned with rows of haricandana, mandāra, and mango trees,
crowded with devadāru trees, and beautified by sarala and arjuna trees,

with black aloe and clove trees, with bowers and creeper-cottages,
that best of mountains shines, always giving flowers and fruits.

Having seen that delightful mountain, Bhṛgu, afflicted then by the famine,
made his dwelling right there with a joyful heart.

On that charming mountain, in its caves and forests,
Bhṛgu, fully intent on ascetic practices, performed austerities for a long time.
While the twice-born was thus staying, dwelling in his hermitage, O chief of kings,

a Vidyādhara couple came down from the mountain.
Approaching, they bowed to the sage and stood there, deeply sorrowful.

Seeing the two in such a state, the twice-born spoke sweet words:
"Speak, Vidyādhara, out of affection: why are you two so deeply sorrowful?"

Hearing the sage's words, the Vidyādhara spoke to the twice-born:
"Listen, O best of ascetics, to the cause of my grief.

Having obtained the fruit of good deeds, I reached the abode of the thirty [gods];
though I attained the body of a deity, my face became that of a tiger.

I do not know of what karma this fruition has arrived;
remembering this again and again, my mind finds no peace.

Listen to another matter, O brāhmaṇa, by which my mind is indeed perturbed:
this is my auspicious wife, sweet-voiced and shapely,

skilled in the arts of dance and song, endowed with all good virtues.
When she was an unmarried maiden, then by this stainless one,

the sage Nārada, connoisseur of the melody of playing the vīṇā,
was intensely pleased with the lute and the seven-stringed harp.

Even in her youthful innocence, singing with a melodious throat,
she pleased even the king of the gods, who knows the varied musical notes and sounds.

When she, her body moved by artistic passion, played the lute,
hearing that pañcama tone, sweet with various winding cadences,

Maheśvara was delighted, his hair standing on end, shaking his head.
In character, nobility, array of virtues, beauty, and the wealth of youth,

there is no woman with beautiful hips in heaven who is equal to her.
Where is this goddess-faced lovely woman, and where am I, a tiger-faced man?
"Reflecting thus, O Brahmin, I am continually burned in my heart." / Having heard this spoken by the Vidyādhara, the delight of Ikṣvāku's race,

Bhṛgu, who knows the three times, possessing divine vision, said with a smile:
"Listen, O best of Vidyādharas, to the wondrous fruit of actions."
The wise, when obtaining it, are not bewildered; those bewildered are of ignorant mind. / Just as poison is dreadful even if only the size of a fly's foot,
so an action, even though performed as small, is terrible in its fruition. / Having fasted on the eleventh day [of the fortnight] in the month of Māgha, you applied an oil massage;
on the twelfth day in a former body, by that [act] you became tiger-faced. / Because of having fasted on the holy eleventh day and then resorting to oil on the twelfth day,
Purūravas formerly attained an ugly body in this very way. / Seeing his own foul body, he was stricken with sorrow through that grief.
Having gone to the king of mountains, on the bank of the lake of the deities, / standing with supreme joy, purified, having bathed, seated upon a kuśa grass seat,
dark like a fresh raincloud, with eyes long as lotus petals, / holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, enveloped in yellow garments,
shining with the Kaustubha jewel, wearing a garland of forest flowers, / the king, meditating upon Hari in his heart, having restrained all his senses,
performed severely dreadful asceticism for three months without food. / Pleased with his slight asceticism, worshipped through seven births,
remembering him, [Hari] then manifested Himself directly to that king / on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, when the sun was in Capricorn.
Having quickly anointed that emperor with water from a conch with delight, / Vāsudeva, reminding him of his conduct regarding the oil, granted him
an exceedingly handsome form, charming and captivating the mind, / on account of which the goddess Urvaśī, leader of celestial women, desired him.
Having thus attained his boon, the king went to his city, his purpose fulfilled. / Knowing the course of karma thus, why does the Vidyādhara grieve?
If you wish to remove the deformity caused by the Dānava, / then swiftly, solely upon my word, [perform] the destruction of past sin:
Perform your bathing in the month of Māgha in the waters of the river at Mount Maṇikūṭa, / frequented by sages, Siddhas, and gods. I shall explain to you the rite for it.
By the power of your good fortune, Māgha is near, on the fifth day. / Beginning from the bright eleventh day of the month of Pauṣa, sleeping on bare ground,
fasting for one month, perform bathing at the three junctures of the day. / Worshipping Viṣṇu at the three junctures of the day, having abandoned pleasures, with subdued senses,
until the bright eleventh day of Māgha, O best among Vidyādharas, / thereafter, on the holy day of the twelfth, I shall burn away your sins,
and having sprinkled you with auspicious waters consecrated with mantras, O god, / I shall make your face like the face of Kāma, O sinless one.
Becoming endowed with the face of a deity, O best of Vidyādharas, / sport at your pleasure along with this fair-complexioned woman.
Knowing the majesty of Māgha, always perform the Māgha bath, / so that the fulfillment of your desires will always come to pass.
Thus was told to him by the noble, omniscient Bhṛgu; / to the Vidyādhara, O lord of kings, the verse was again recited.
Destruction of misfortune comes by Māgha baths; extinction of sin comes by Māgha baths. / Māgha is superior to all sacrifices; it yields the fruit of all gifts.
Māgha roars above sacrifices, and Māgha roars above yoga; / Māgha roars above fierce asceticism, O Vidyādhara!
At Puṣkara and Kurukṣetra, at Brahmāvarta and Pṛthūdaka, / at Avimukta and Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—
whatever fruit is obtained by men through observances in ten years, / that fruit is obtained in Māgha by bathing for three days; there is no doubt.
Those in whose minds there is a long-standing desire for the heavenly world / must bathe in any water whatever when the sun is in Capricorn.
Longevity, health, prosperity, beauty, good fortune, and virtues— / those whose desire is for these must not abandon the immersion in Māgha.
And those who fear hell, and those who fear accumulated poverty— / by them an immersion in Māgha must by all means be performed with effort.
And for washing away the mire of poverty, sin, and misfortune, / there is no other means than the Māgha bath, O best of kings.
Actions devoid of faith indeed bear very little fruit; / [yet] the Māgha bath, performed in whatever way, gives complete fruit.
Without desire or with desire, in any outdoor water whatsoever, / one who bathes in Māgha experiences no sorrows here or in the world beyond.
Just as in the two fortnights the moon waxes and wanes, / so sin wanes in Māgha, and the heap of merit increases.
And just as various gems are produced from a mine, / so merits are produced for men from the Māgha bath.
Just as the wish-yielding cow grants whatever is desired and the Cintāmaṇi whatever is thought of, / so the Māgha bath here gives all desires.
Asceticism is supreme in the Kṛta age, supreme knowledge in the Tretā age, / and sacrificial worship in the Dvāpara age; knowledge is supreme in the Kali age, but Māgha in all ages.
Indeed, for all castes and all stages of life, O king, / the Māgha bath showers down with torrents of dharma.
Vasiṣṭha said: / Hearing this speech of Bhṛgu, in that very hermitage, the divine being / together with Bhṛgu in the month of Māgha, on the mountain by the bank of a stream,
performed the bath together with his wife according to the prescribed rule. / Then, through the grace of Bhṛgu, having attained his heart's desire,
becoming one with a deity's face, he rejoiced on the jewel-mountain. / Bhṛgu, having shown favor to him, went rejoiced to the Vindhya.

On the king of jewel-mountains, by mere bathing in Māgha, the Vidyādhara became endowed with a face and form like the god of love. / Bhṛgu too, having his body worn by observances, descended from the foot of the Vindhya and went with his disciples to the Revā.

This glorification of Māgha, the essence of the entire universe, was spoken to the Vidyādhara by the best of the twice-born, Bhṛgu, O king. / Whoever hears it daily, astonishing with its varied fruits, would obtain all pleasant desires like a god.

Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the glorification of Māgha, / in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa, ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter.

6.126.m: Vasiṣṭha said: / Now I shall proclaim the glorification of Māgha, O best of kings, / as spoken by Dattātreya to Kārtavīrya who questioned him.
Going to Dattātreya, Hari in visible form, who resided on Mount Sahya, / the king, lord of Māhiṣmatī, questioned that twice-born one.
Sahasrārjuna said: / O holy one, best among yogins, all dharmas have been heard by me. / Tell me, by your grace, the fruit of the Māgha bath, O you of noble vows.
Dattātreya said: / Let this auspicious answer to your question be heard, O tiger among kings, / which was formerly spoken by Brahmā to the great-souled Nārada.
I shall recount all that great fruit of the Māgha bath, / according to place, according to sacred ford, according to rule, and according to practice.
In this Bhāratavarṣa, particularly in this realm of actions, / the birth of men who do not bathe in Māgha is declared to be fruitless.
Just as the sky without the sun, or the circle of stars without the moon, / so a good action does not shine without the Māgha bath, O king.
Hari is not pleased by vows, gifts, and austerities / as Keśava is pleased by the mere immersion in Māgha.
There is no splendor equal to solar splendor; / similarly, rites born of sacrifices are not equal to the bath of Māgha.
For the gratification of Vāsudeva, for the removal of all sins, / and for attaining heaven, a human being should perform the Māgha bath.
What is the use of guarding a body, even if well nourished and powerful, / if it is impermanent, impure, and without the bath of Māgha?
With bones as its pillars, bound by sinews, smeared with flesh and blood, / covered with skin, foul-smelling, and a vessel of urine and feces;
pervaded by old age, grief, and misfortune, an abode of diseases, afflicted, / full of passion, impermanent, and the dwelling of all defects;
afflicted by the torment of troubling others, hostile to others, extremely poisonous, / greedy, treacherous, cruel, ungrateful, and fleeting;
hard to satisfy, difficult to maintain, corrupt, endowed with the three humors, / discharging impurities, full of orifices, and deluded by the three afflictions;
by nature delighting in unrighteousness, agitated by hundreds of cravings, / and standing at the gate of hell through desire, anger, and great greed;
in the end, it becomes worms, feces, or ashes, the food of dogs. / Such a body is indeed useless if bereft of the bath of Māgha.
Like bubbles upon the water, like fleas among living creatures, / they are born only to die, who are bereft of the bath of Māgha.
A brāhmaṇa who is not a Vaiṣṇava is ruined; a funeral rite without a yogin is ruined; / a holy site devoid of piety is ruined; a family lacking good conduct is ruined.
Righteousness accompanied by hypocrisy is ruined; penance is ruined by anger alone; / knowledge that is not steadfast is ruined; and sacred learning is ruined by negligence.
A woman devoid of devotion to elders is ruined; a celibate student is ruined by her; / an oblation offered in an rekindled fire is ruined; an enjoyment without a witness is ruined.
A maiden made a source of livelihood is ruined; cooking for oneself is ruined; / a sacrifice performed with a Śūdra's alms is ruined; a miser's wealth is ruined.
Learning without practice is ruined; a king who creates conflict is ruined; / a sacred ford used for livelihood is ruined; a vow taken for livelihood is ruined.
Speech tainted by untruth is ruined, and so is malicious gossip; / a mantra that is doubtful is ruined; recitation with an agitated mind is ruined.
A gift given to one unlearned in the Veda is ruined; and a faithless person is ruined; / everything done regarding the other world without faith is ruined.
Just as the present world is ruined for the impoverished, O king, / so the life of human beings is ruined without the bath of Māgha.
When the sun resides in Capricorn, he who does not bathe before sunrise— / how could he be freed from sins, and how could he go to heaven?
The killer of a brāhmaṇa, the thief of gold, the drinker of liquor, the defiler of the guru's bed, / and the fifth who associates with them—one who bathes in Māgha becomes free from sin.
In the month of Māgha, the waters call out as the sun begins to rise: / 'Whom among the trembling shall we purify—the slayer of a brāhmaṇa, or the drinker of liquor?'
All minor sins and even great crimes / are reduced to ashes for a man intent on the bath of Māgha.
All sins tremble at the approach of the bath of Māgha, [crying:] / 'This is the time of our destruction, if he will bathe in the water!'
Thus sins lament on seeing a man prepared for the bath. / Best of men shine like fires through the baths of Māgha.
Freed from all sins, just like the moon from clouds— / whether wet or dry, slight or severe, committed by speech, mind, or deeds—
the bath of Māgha burns away sin just as fire burns faggots. / Whatever sin was committed inadvertently, or through knowledge or ignorance,
that is destroyed merely by bathing when the sun resides in Capricorn. / The sinless go to heaven, and the most sinful attain purity.
No doubt should be held in this matter, O ruler of men, regarding the bath of Māgha; / all are qualified in Māgha, just as in devotion to Viṣṇu, O king.
Māgha grants heaven to all; it destroys the sins of all. / This indeed is the supreme mantra; this indeed is supreme penance.
And this bath of Māgha is the supreme, unexcelled expiation. / The inclination for the bath of Māgha arises in men from practice in previous births,
just as skill in spiritual knowledge comes from practice across births, O king, / which is expert at washing away the smeared mud of cyclic existence.
The bath of Māgha is the purifier among purifiers and supreme, O king. / Those who bathe in Māgha, which grants the fruit of all desires, O king—
how they enjoy pleasures resembling the moon, sun, and planets! / Hear, O king, the great marvel arising from the power of the bath of Māgha:
An auspicious brāhmaṇa woman named Kubjikā, born in the lineage of Bhṛgu, / tormented by the grief of early widowhood, performed penance that was extremely difficult to endure.
At the foot of the Vindhya range, in the great holy site at the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā, / she took vows there, wholly devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Always possessing good conduct, ever free from worldly attachment, / having conquered her senses, having subdued anger, truthful, and speaking little;
well-mannered, generous, and dedicated to emaciating the body; / offering to the ancestors, deities, and twice-born, and sacrificing likewise into the fire;
she ate only at the sixth mealtime, always subsisting on gleaned grains, O king, / through vows such as the kṛcchra, atikṛcchra, pārāka, and taptakṛcchra.
She spent the auspicious months on the bank of the Narmadā. / Thus, by that ascetic woman wearing bark garments, endowed with good character,
possessing great strength of mind, and endowed with fortitude and contentment, / sixty Māgha baths were performed at the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā.
Then, emaciated by asceticism, she died in that holy site, O king. / By that merit born of the bath of Māgha, she in the realm of Viṣṇu
dwelt full of joy for a thousand cycles of four yugas. / Later, for the destruction of Sunda and Upasunda, from the Lotus-born [Brahmā] again,
she was brought down into the world of Brahmā under the name Tilottamā. / By that remainder of her merit, she became the singular abode of beauty.
Not born from a womb, a jewel among women, fascinating even to the gods, / a slender woman, a lake of charm, she became the foremost of the apsarases.
She was truly a marvel created by the skilled creator, the Ordainer. / Having brought her forth, the Creator, pleased, then gave her permission:
'O fawn-eyed one, go quickly for the destruction of the Daityas!' / Then that lovely woman, departing from the world of Brahmā and taking a vīṇā,
went by way of the sky to where those two enemies of the gods were. / Having bathed there in the pure, clear water of the Revā,
and having put on a red garment with the radiance of a bandhūka blossom, / her bracelets jingling, her girdle and anklets ringing charmingly,
with a swaying pearl necklace at her neck, splendid with moving earrings, / wearing a crest of mādhavī flowers, she stood on a bough of an aśoka tree,
singing sweetly and playing the vīṇā, / modulating the six notes, exceedingly melodious, tender, and indistinctly sweet.
Thus the maiden Tilottamā, standing in the aśoka grove, / pleasing to the heart like a digit of the moon, was seen by the Daitya soldiers.
Seeing her, O king, the soldiers, filled with great astonishment and joy, / hastening without her noticing, went to Sunda and Upasunda
and reported with great agitation, describing her again and again: / 'O two Daityas, we do not know whether she is a goddess or a dānava woman!
Or is she a Nāga maiden, or a Yakṣī? She is indeed the jewel among women in every way! / You two are the enjoyers of jewels in the world, and that maiden is truly a jewel.
She is not far off ahead, in the aśoka grove, dispelling sorrow. / Go and quickly look upon her, who enchants even the god of love!'
Thus, hearing the charming words of the commanders, / leaving behind the goblet of liquor and giving up the sprinkling of water,
and leaving thousands of excellent women, from that body of water, / taking cruel iron maces weighing a hundred bhāras, resembling the rod of Death,
each taking their own, they ran forward in haste / to where she stood, adorned in erotic splendor, like Caṇḍī ready to kill.
O King, as if fanning the fire of love of the two Daityas, / standing before her, the two wretched ones were bewitched by her beauty.
Intoxicated especially with wine, they spoke to one another: / 'Brother, desist! Let this fair-complexioned woman be my wife.'
'Noble one, you alone must give up this intoxicating-eyed woman for me, to be my wife!' / Thus enraged by obstinacy, like two wild elephants in rut,
destined by time, they struck each other with maces; / by their mutual blows, deprived of life, they fell upon the earth.
Seeing them dead, a great uproar was made by the soldiers: / 'Who is this like the Night of Destruction? Alas, what is this that has arrived?'
While the troops were speaking thus, Tilottamā, having cast down / the two Daityas, Sunda and Upasunda, upon the mountain peak like lightning,
quickly departed into the sky, illuminating the ten directions. / Having thus accomplished the work of the gods, she came before Brahmā.
Then, commended by the pleased god Brahmā, [she was told]: / 'A place in the chariot of the sun has been given to you by me, O moon-faced one.
Enjoy manifold pleasures as long as the sun remains in the sky.' / In this way that brahmin woman, O king, having become the best of Apsarases,
even today enjoys in the world of the sun the great fruit of the Māgha bath. / Therefore, O king, with effort, by faithful men
a bath must always be taken when the sun is in Capricorn by those desiring the supreme state. / For him there is no goal of life unattained here.
There is no sin that is not destroyed for a man who plunges [into water] in Māgha; / all sacrifices accompanied by gifts do not equal that.
By the Māgha bath, O lord of kings, especially at a sacred place, / there is no other action that gives heaven, no other that destroys sin,

since on earth there is nothing else that grants liberation equal to the Māgha bath.'

Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, / in the glorification of Māgha, in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa, in the praise of the bath in Māgha, [ends the chapter] named "The Slaying of the Daityas Sunda and Upasunda."
